commentary.bottom_line: Seven studies test scope enforcement, and all but one are simulations or automated benchmarks. They suggest that refusal instructions and scope controls can raise correct refusals, sometimes at a cost to answering legitimate questions, but none tests multi-turn drift or the usefulness of redirection in live care.

perspectives.view: Six of seven tests are level 4 or 5 simulations or benchmarks. The one real deployment involved 8 pharmacy leaders and reported no numbers. Refusal rose from 0/30 at baseline to 90% to 100% with refusal instructions, but only on single-turn queries. Indirectness, small samples, and missing rates support very low certainty.

Hazard studies report that 61.4% of conversations that began with a safe response later collapsed to unsafe, and that jailbreak success reached 82.1% under role-play and multi-turn prompting. Among tests of the practice, a safety system prompt raised safety-appropriate rates by 5.9 points under adversarial caregiver pressure. No test examined cumulative multi-turn drift.

Adding an out-of-distribution classifier raised appropriate refusal from 0.94 to 0.97 and cut utility on legitimate questions from 0.86 to 0.69. Separate benchmarks found safety-optimised models refusing up to 80% of hard benign prompts, and one model reached 16% accuracy because of over-refusal. Testing may therefore need to measure over-refusal alongside refusal.

One test used Thai-language questions and found that removing the safety prompt led the model to produce a full drug-dosing schedule. Hazard studies in Japanese and Chinese settings show safety declining over conversation turns. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users.

A regulatory discussion paper lists adversarial prompting, prompt injection, emotional manipulation, and multi-turn drift as possible testing, using permissive language. The tests of the practice cover single-turn and benchmark adversarial queries. None follows the multi-turn cumulative drift scenario the paper describes.

One agent system with process-boundary governance blocked all adversarial and out-of-scope requests across three datasets regardless of the model used. This suggests that scope controls placed outside the model may carry over when vendors change models. Another system averaged 5.3 seconds per response. Neither study reported staffing or cost.

In one simulation, chatbots endorsed 32% of harmful proposals rather than setting limits or redirecting. Another study found that models often fail to redirect false-premise questions even after detecting the premise. No test measured whether a refusal pointed patients to a clinician or other human help.

commentary.research_gap: No study tests scope enforcement under multi-turn adversarial conversation in a deployed clinical tool. No study measures whether refusals give useful redirection to a human or an appropriate resource. The trade-off between correct refusal and over-refusal has been measured in only one benchmark of 136 questions.
commentary.underserved_note: One test of the practice used Thai-language questions, which covers a non-English population in a benchmark setting only. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy users. Health systems serving these patients therefore have no direct evidence on how scope controls perform for them.
